subject: Observability benchmark
summary:
The checkout slowdown was caused by severe internal latency in the **order-service** between ~01:20 and 02:10 UTC on 2026-10-29 (about 6 hours before the question). Order-service P95 latency spiked from a normal ~48ms baseline to **10 seconds** (histogram ceiling). Trace-level evidence proves the bottleneck was inside the order-service itself — not in its downstream dependencies. In trace `00f1b1940a94a193ea48c57e693863bb` (15.2 s total), the user-service child call completed in only 25 ms, yet the order-service span consumed 10.96 s. CPU and memory of the order-service were normal throughout, and request volume did not surge, which together point to internal resource contention (e.g., connection-pool or thread-pool exhaustion) rather than load or downstream degradation. The user-service had its own earlier spike (22:20–23:00 UTC on Oct 28) but was healthy during the main checkout incident. The payment-service had only a minor, isolated spike at 01:50 UTC.

**Representative trace ID:** `00f1b1940a94a193ea48c57e693863bb`

impact.summary: Checkout (POST /api/orders and related endpoints) experienced P95 latency of up to 10 seconds from ~01:20 to ~02:10 UTC on 2026-10-29, with intermittent elevated latency persisting until ~04:40 UTC. Some requests returned 5xx errors (502, 503, 500). Normal baseline was ~48ms; peak was a ~200x degradation. Customer-facing checkout was severely impacted for approximately 50 minutes, with residual slowness for several more hours.

findings.statement: Order-service was the primary bottleneck: its internal processing time accounted for the vast majority of end-to-end latency, while downstream calls (user-service, payment-service) were fast.
findings.mechanism: The order-service span consumed 10.96s of the 15.2s trace while its only downstream call (user-service) completed in 25ms, proving the time was spent blocked inside the order-service — not waiting on dependencies. CPU and memory were normal, pointing to internal resource contention (connection pool exhaustion, thread pool saturation, or lock contention) as the blocking mechanism.

findings.statement: Order-service P95 latency spiked from ~48ms to 10 seconds between 01:20-02:00 UTC on Oct 29, with additional intermittent spikes (0.5-1.8s) through 04:40 UTC.
findings.mechanism: Prometheus histogram_quantile P95 for order-service rose from ~48ms baseline to 10s (histogram ceiling) between 01:20 and 02:00 UTC, with residual spikes (0.5-1.8s) continuing until ~04:40 UTC.

findings.statement: Representative trace 00f1b1940a94a193ea48c57e693863bb (15.2s) shows the order-service span consumed 10.96s while user-service took only 25ms, proving internal blocking.
findings.mechanism: Trace data shows 4 spans: webapp (15.2s) -> api-gateway (13.7s) -> order-service (10.96s) -> user-service (25ms). The user-service call was fast; the delay was entirely within order-service.

findings.statement: Trace 0595f4e097fcacc5724644e76d76ad60 (8.1s) shows order-service error (5.86s) with a fast but errored user-service call (25ms), confirming order-service internal failure.
findings.mechanism: Trace shows a POST /api/orders taking 8.1s total with order-service span at 5.86s (error status) and user-service call at 25ms (error status).

findings.statement: Order-service CPU and memory remained stable and low during the latency spike, ruling out CPU or memory saturation as the cause.
findings.mechanism: CPU rate stayed at ~0.0015 CPU-s/s and memory at ~115-122 MB throughout the spike, showing no resource saturation at the process level.

findings.statement: Order-service logs confirm HTTP 500/502/503 errors and extreme request durations (up to 14,190ms) during the spike window, including 'upstream service error' and 'request failed' messages.
findings.mechanism: Loki logs show order-service returning 502, 503, and 500 errors during the spike window, with request durations of 4.9s, 6.7s, 10.3s, and 14.2s.

findings.statement: User-service had an earlier severe P95 latency spike (9-10s) from 22:20-23:00 UTC on Oct 28, predating the main order-service incident, and another 4.25s spike at 00:25 UTC.
findings.mechanism: User-service had its own P95 spike to 9-10s from 22:20-23:00 UTC on Oct 28 and a 4.25s spike at 00:25 UTC Oct 29, but was at normal latency (~48ms) during the main 01:20-02:00 checkout incident.

findings.statement: Payment-service had a minor isolated P95 spike to 2.2s at 01:50 UTC but was otherwise normal during the checkout slowdown.
findings.mechanism: Payment-service P95 spiked to 2.2s only at 01:50 UTC and was otherwise at ~48ms baseline during the main incident window.

hypotheses.statement: Order-service internal resource pool exhaustion (connection pool or thread pool) caused blocking without CPU or memory pressure
hypotheses.test: Check order-service connection pool metrics, thread pool metrics, or add instrumentation for DB query latency to confirm pool exhaustion vs lock contention

hypotheses.statement: Earlier user-service degradation cascaded into order-service connection pool exhaustion via accumulated slow in-flight requests
hypotheses.test: Correlate user-service recovery time with order-service connection pool state; check if order-service retains connections to user-service after the downstream recovered

actions.title: Investigate order-service internal resource pools
actions.rationale: The trace evidence shows the delay is inside order-service with fast downstream calls and no CPU/memory pressure, strongly suggesting connection or thread pool exhaustion. Confirming this identifies the exact fix.
actions.verification: Pool metrics or config shows pool size was insufficient for concurrent load during the spike, or logs show pool exhaustion/timeout messages.

actions.title: Add timeout and pool-exhaustion metrics to order-service
actions.rationale: The 10s histogram ceiling suggests requests may be hitting a hard timeout. Knowing the timeout helps distinguish between slow processing and timeout-abandoned requests.
actions.verification: New metrics appear in Prometheus and can be queried for correlation with latency spikes.

actions.title: Review order-service error handling for connection leaks
actions.rationale: The root cause of the pool exhaustion is unknown - it could be a slow leak, a sudden traffic pattern, or a dependency causing requests to hold resources longer than expected.
actions.verification: Static analysis or code review identifies at least one path where a connection is not returned on error.

limitations.statement: No connection pool or thread pool metrics were available in Prometheus, so the specific internal resource (DB connection pool, thread pool, lock) that caused blocking cannot be confirmed from metrics alone.
Loki log queries with regex filters failed due to the read budget being exhausted, so full error log analysis during the spike was incomplete.
The http_requests_total metric for order-service returned only one series without a code label breakdown, preventing error-rate quantification by HTTP status code.
No database-level metrics (query latency, connection count) were discoverable in Prometheus, so DB-side contribution to the blocking cannot be confirmed or ruled out.
